title: EUBRL: Epistemic Uncertainty Directed Bayesian Reinforcement Learning
claim: Our method matches or beats baselines in success rate and sample efficiency as problem size grows, especially under stochastic dynamics.
layout: 2x2 grid: bar charts above, scatter plots below, deterministic left, stochastic right
description: A 2x2 grid of plots on the DeepSea exploration task. The top row has grouped bar charts of success rate (0 to 1) at problem sizes 10, 20 and 50. The left panel is titled 'DeepSea Deterministic' and the right panel 'DeepSea Stochastic'. Bars are colored by method: blue PSRL, cyan BEB, yellow VBRB, green RMAX, red EUBRL, and purple EUBRL+ in the stochastic panel only. PSRL fails at larger sizes. The bottom row has scatter plots of average episodes to solve the task against problem size, with different markers per method and a legend inside each panel. PSRL needs the most episodes, and the dashed Uniform baseline blows up exponentially in the deterministic panel. EUBRL and RMAX sit lowest. The eye goes first to the bright bar clusters, then to the scatter markers. The caption describes a summary of tasks, but the figure shows results.
caption: Success rate and average episodes to solve task, reported for both deterministic and stochastic variants over different problem sizes (S = N × N). Averaged over 20 random seeds.
abstract: At the boundary between the known and the unknown, an agent inevitably confronts the dilemma of whether to explore or to exploit. Epistemic uncertainty reflects such boundaries, representing systematic uncertainty due to limited knowledge. In this paper, we propose a Bayesian reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm, $\texttt{EUBRL}$, which leverages epistemic guidance to achieve principled exploration. This guidance adaptively reduces per-step regret arising from estimation errors. We establish nearly minimax-optimal regret and sample complexity guarantees for a class of sufficiently expressive priors in infinite-horizon discounted MDPs. Empirically, we evaluate $\texttt{EUBRL}$ on tasks characterized by sparse rewards, long horizons, and stochasticity. Results demonstrate that $\texttt{EUBRL}$ achieves superior sample efficiency, scalability, and consistency.
